subject: Biology
title: How Birds Navigate
description: A micro-lesson that makes How Birds Navigate usable.

hook.text: An Arctic tern flies from the Arctic to Antarctica and back every year—a 70,000 km round trip.

buildup.text: Migratory birds use the sun, stars, and Earth's magnetic field to navigate.

discovery.text: Pigeons have magnetite crystals in their beaks that sense magnetic field direction.

twist.text: Young birds learn routes from experienced adults, but some species navigate alone on their first trip.

climax.text: Light pollution and communication towers confuse migrating birds, killing millions each year.

punchline.text: A bird's GPS runs on magnets, stars, and instinct.

quiz.question: What helps pigeons sense Earth's magnetic field?

details.summary: Birds use multiple navigation systems including Earth's magnetic field, star patterns, the sun's position, landmarks, and even smell. Migratory birds combine these cues to travel thousands of kilometers with remarkable accuracy across hemispheres.
details.whyItMatters: Avian navigation reveals sensory abilities beyond human perception. The discovery that birds sense magnetic fields through quantum effects in their eyes connects animal behavior to quantum physics in unexpected ways.
takeaways: Birds detect Earth's magnetic field using cryptochrome proteins in their eyes
Young birds learn star maps during their first summer for night navigation
Multiple redundant navigation systems provide backup when one fails

faq.question: How do birds sense Earth's magnetic field?
faq.answer: The leading theory involves cryptochrome proteins in the retina that are sensitive to magnetic fields through quantum radical pair reactions. Birds may literally see the magnetic field as a visual overlay on their normal vision.

faq.question: Can young birds navigate without experienced adults?
faq.answer: Some species can. Cuckoo chicks raised by foster parents migrate solo to the correct wintering grounds using innate magnetic compass directions. Other species like cranes require cultural learning from experienced birds to find specific routes.
